Not upgraded to A because the measured build is not pinned to a commit: the results predate the commits that hold them, the Rust kernels were replaced by assembler templates around the measurement (f8aa157, 2026-09-29), and HEAD (7df1749, 2026-09-30) changed the Node code path for large inputs, so the current harness on the current code does not reproduce the large-input Node rows.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: No external compiler for the SHA-2/SHA-1/MD5/PBKDF2 kernels: hand-written WebAssembly emitted by the in-repo assembler (wasm/kernels.mjs, wasm/asm.mjs) and expanded at first use; scrypt ROMix assembled from wasm/scrypt.wat with binaryen (^132.0.0 devDependency); WASM SIMD required. Benchmarks run as node --expose-gc --max-old-space-size=8192 via bench/interleave.mjs on Node 24.16, plus headless Chromium 149.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on a days-old repository with 1 star (published numbers measured 2026-09-28). The record's earlier worry that the Node column measures OpenSSL does not hold for the published numbers: they were measured before commit 7df1749 (2026-09-30) added the node:crypto path for one-shot inputs of 64 KiB or more, and the measured Node sha256 1 MB time (2.12 ms, about 494 MB/s, the same as in Chromium) is the WASM kernel, not SHA-NI OpenSSL. The reverse problem applies now: the current 1.8.2 package hands large one-shot hashes in Node to node:crypto, so the large-input Node rows describe an older code path, and the README tables were not re-measured after that change. The root README summary table disagrees with its own results table (scrypt 3.1x vs 2.3x measured, pbkdf2 3.3-5.7x vs 3.4x/7.2x, md5 6.9x vs 7.8x). The only baseline is pure-JS @noble/hashes 1.8.0; hash-wasm, node:crypto and WebCrypto, which are much faster on large inputs, are not compared. Short-input gains are smaller for streaming (sha256 64 KB in 100 B updates 1.2x, hmac sha256 1.3x). Each row keeps the best (minimum) per-process median of 3 interleaved fresh-process rounds. The package LICENSE still says the kernels are re-implemented in Rust (rust/src), but that directory is gone (replaced by wasm templates in f8aa157). Before f8aa157, bundled builds silently ran noble's JS because the wasm init was marked /* @__PURE__ */. SHA-3, BLAKE, RIPEMD-160 and Argon2 run noble's code unchanged (1.0x). The repo URL points at the package directory of R1ck404/fast-packages.

notes: Every claimed number matches the README results table and the committed raw files, both Node and Chromium columns. Shortcomings to record: first-party only, 1 star, days old; pure-JS noble is the only baseline; the README tables predate HEAD's native node:crypto path, so the large-input Node rows no longer describe what the shipped package runs; the README summary table contradicts the measured table (scrypt 3.1x vs 2.3x); the LICENSE text describes the removed Rust kernels. Could be argued up to A (public harness, CPU, runtime versions, no external compiler for the hash kernels) if reproduction from git history at f8aa157/73a1829 is accepted.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust (toolchain version not stated) via cargo build --release for wasm32-unknown-unknown: opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1, panic="abort" (rust/Cargo.toml); rustflags -C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory,+sign-ext,+mutable-globals,+nontrapping-fptoint, -C no-vectorize-loops, -C llvm-args=-unroll-max-count=1 (rust/.cargo/config.toml); then wasm-opt (binaryen) in build.mjs. Benchmarks run as node --expose-gc --max-old-space-size=8192 via bench/interleave.mjs on Node 24.16.
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on a repository that is only days old (oldest visible commits 2026-09-27, result files from 2026-09-26/28) with 1 star. Each row keeps the best (minimum) per-process median of 3 interleaved fresh-process rounds; raw data is in results/. The published tables were measured 2026-09-28, before commit 7df1749 (2026-09-30) changed rust/src/deflate.rs (level-0 stored path) and the shipped wasm; the README tables were not re-measured. The only baseline is pako 2.1.0; native Node zlib, zlib-ng and fflate are not compared (fflate and pako 3.0.2 sit in the devDependencies but are not in the published tables), so it is a win over the JS equivalent and not over native zlib. The deflate L6/L9 gains are about 2x and, per the README, bounded by zlib's match finder (output is byte-identical to pako). The 20x row (deflate level 6 on 75 B) and the other tiny-input rows mostly measure pako's per-call setup, not compression throughput. The repo covers several packages (fast-acorn, fast-esbuild-wasm, fast-es-module-lexer, fast-brotli-wasm, fast-noble-hashes); this entry is the zlib port only, and the repo URL points at its package directory. fast-pako throws where pako would loop forever or corrupt data on some invalid options (documented differences).

notes: Every claimed number matches the README and the committed results file (ungzip typescript 99.84 vs 17.25 ms, inflate 9 MB 28.13 vs 6.70 ms, deflateRaw L1 9.85 vs 3.24 ms, L6 32.80 vs 15.70 ms, L9 140.21 vs 64.33 ms, 75 B 80.6 vs 4.0 us; the import-plus-first-ungzip row is from the README startup table). Shortcomings to record: first-party only, 1 star, days old; pako is the only baseline (no native zlib or fflate); tables predate HEAD's deflate changes; Rust toolchain version unstated; tiny-input 20x reflects pako setup cost. License MIT AND Zlib confirmed from packages/fast-pako/package.json and LICENSE.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: WASM: emcc --bind -std=c++14 src/wasm.cpp -s WASM=1 -s SINGLE_FILE=1 -O3 (package.json build:wasm; Emscripten version not stated). Addon: node-gyp rebuild --release with default node-gyp Release flags (binding.gyp sets no extra flags). Node version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Toy kernels with +-8-15% reported variance; no CPU, Node version or Emscripten version stated, and the README labels the pure-JS version 'Native'. WebAssembly is fastest on only 2 of 5 tasks (Fibonacci, Fermat); it beats pure JS on 3 of 5 (also SHA256, 34,445 vs 13,453 ops/s, about 2.6x derived from page data) but loses to JS on Levenshtein and linear regression and to the N-API addon on Levenshtein, regression and SHA256. The Fibonacci kernel is tail-recursive, which the C++ compiler turns into a loop while JS has no tail calls, so that row mostly measures tail-call elimination. benchmark.js draws random inputs on every call and its randomInRange helper ignores its min argument (Fibonacci n ranges 0-45, not 30-45); inputs are identically distributed for all three implementations. A benchmark/demo repository rather than a reusable library; last release 0.0.13 (2019-05-06), last commit 2022-04-09. The linked Medium post was not opened (blocked).

notes: README numbers match the record exactly. Shortcomings to record: no CPU, Node or Emscripten version; noisy toy kernels; WASM loses to plain JS on 2 of 5 and to the native addon on 3 of 5; Fibonacci row measures tail-call elimination; randomInRange min bug; benchmark repo, not a library; abandoned (last commit 2022-04-09). Metadata confirmed: MIT (LICENSE.md), 196 stars, 12 forks, not a fork.
